column4: “Your Lord creates what He wills and chooses; they have no choice” joins making to the assignment of an outcome and places selection with the Creator rather than with those drawing a lot.
God creates everything on earth, turns to heaven, and proportions it as seven heavens; creation proceeds into the ordered finishing of a constructed whole.
God proportions the heaven as seven heavens, assigns each its command, and calls the result the determination of the Mighty, the Knowing; it completes the measured provisioning of 41:10.
God describes proportioning the human form before breathing spirit into it, making تسوية a preparatory stage with a directed completion.
The repeated declaration that God will proportion the human before breathing spirit into him preserves the same craft sequence in a second passage.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it presents the inner person as a deliberately fitted creation.
After the soul is proportioned in 91:7, it is inspired with both its wickedness and its piety; fitted creation is followed by disclosure of the two possible directions.
“Remind, for the reminder benefits the believers” directly resolves 87:9’s conditional wording and also returns the ordinary Quranic sense of نفع to the root used for a water-skin side piece.
God says He made the revelation easy on the Prophet’s tongue so he could give good news and warn, closely matching ease granted to the messenger for the work of reminder.
God has made the Quran easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember; ease and effective reminder are made one act.
The repeated statement that the Quran is made easy for remembrance supplies another explicit occurrence of the same ease-to-reminder relation.
This third refrain again joins divine easing of the Quran to the possibility of taking reminder, confirming that the formulation governs successive warning scenes.
The fourth refrain preserves the same promise that a made-easy revelation can become remembrance for a receptive hearer.
God says He made the Quran easy in the Prophet’s tongue so that people might remember; the messenger’s ease is explicitly for remembrance.
Whoever fears God is given ease in his affair, joining the fearing recipient of reminder to divinely prepared ease.
God desires ease rather than hardship, commands completion of the numbered period, and calls for magnifying Him because He guided; ease, measure, guidance, and glorification converge.
If the Prophet speaks aloud, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden; this closely repeats 87:7’s pairing of the overt (الجهر) with the hidden.
Every people receives the command to worship God and avoid false gods; the same ayah then distinguishes those God guided from those upon whom error took hold, joining avoidance to direction.
Abraham asks his Lord to keep him and his children away from idol worship; the surah’s named patriarch voices a positive form of the avoidance root.
Those who avoid false gods and turn back to God receive good news, showing avoidance as a saving orientation rather than the wretched person’s avoidance of reminder.
The Abraham identified in 16:120 is chosen and guided to a straight path, directly connecting the surah’s named patriarch with fitted direction.
God guides Moses and Aaron to the straight path; the Moses named in 37:114 and in Surah 87’s closing scrolls is given the section’s directed course.
Moses offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he might fear, joining guidance, lordship, and the fear that makes reminder effective.
God guides the human to the path, whether he becomes grateful or ungrateful; one directed way opens into opposed human responses.
Every soul’s death has a written appointed term, and the ayah then gives worldly reward to its seeker and afterlife reward to its seeker; limit, selection, and allotted return occur together.
Whoever desires worldly reward is told that both worldly and afterlife reward are with God, relocating the chooser’s sought share within the giver’s larger store.
Those who buy worldly life with the Hereafter enact the section’s choice as an exchange, and their punishment is neither lightened nor relieved.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter and divert from God’s way combine the lower choice with a crooked course.
Because they preferred worldly life over the Hereafter, God does not guide them; the wrong chosen share and the loss of direction are causally joined.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who turns from God’s reminder and desires only worldly life, directly joining failed reminder to the lower choice.
This is called the limit of their knowledge, while the Lord best knows who strays and who is guided; it gives 53:29’s choice both a boundary and a directional judgment.
Men and women each receive an obligatory allotted share from what parents and relatives leave, whether little or much; the share is fixed rather than won by chance.
This ayah specifies further fractional shares for spouses and siblings, extending 4:11’s divine apportionment with distinct, bounded portions.
Men have a share of what they earn and women have a share of what they earn, while all are told to ask God for His bounty; portion and giver remain distinct.
People invent restrictions on cattle and crops, allowing only whomever they choose to consume them; their arbitrary allocation continues the false division exposed in 6:136.
They assign what is in certain animals’ wombs to their males, exclude their wives, and share it only if stillborn; human whim intrudes on both hidden creation and allotment.
The question whether humans receive males while assigning females to God states the proposed division that 53:22 identifies as unjust.
Twelve springs emerge and every people knows its drinking place; water is divided into recognized shares for a whole community.
The twelve tribes receive twelve springs and each people knows its drinking place, repeating the scene of apportioned access to water.
Everyone upon the earth will pass away, supplying the finite endpoint against which any worldly allotment must be measured.
The face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains after 55:26’s universal passing, identifying what outlasts every used-up share.
Every thing perishes except God’s face, while judgment belongs to Him and all return to Him; passing possession, final decision, and endpoint meet in one ayah.
The believer calls worldly life only temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting home, explicitly measuring the two offered destinations.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while lasting righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; the apparent share is weighed against what remains.
Gold and comparable splendor are only worldly enjoyment, while the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing; the “highest” material lot is displaced by the enduring award.
Moses sees a fire and hopes either to bring a brand or “find guidance at the fire”; fire and هدى meet explicitly, illuminating the dictionary image of a fire-straightened guiding staff.
God makes fire for people from the green tree and they kindle from it, presenting fire as a divinely prepared usable material.
The question about the fire people kindle introduces fire as a humanly used tool whose source is then traced to divine making.
God asks whether people created the fire’s tree or He did, relocating the useful flame inside the Creator’s craft.
God makes the fire a reminder and a provision for travelers, joining its practical benefit to its work as remembrance.
After the useful fire of 56:71–73, the command is to glorify the name of the Lord, the Great; crafted provision culminates in the same form of command as 87:1.
“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Great” is a direct repeated command with the same speaker, object, and act as 87:1.
The closing command to glorify the name of the Lord, the Great supplies another exact speaker-level parallel to the surah’s opening command.
Flood foam and smelting dross vanish, while what benefits people remains; useful material, fire-work, benefit, and endurance meet in a single craftsman-like parable.
Pharaoh claims “I am your lord, the highest,” a direct false reversal of the true “your Lord, the Most High” whom the surah commands the Prophet to glorify.
Immediately after idols are said unable to create even a fly, people are said not to appraise God with His true appraisal; created power and failed human measuring confront each other.
People do not appraise God with His true appraisal, while the whole earth and folded heavens display His scale; human estimation fails before the divine measurer’s cosmic grasp.
Those who deny revelation are said not to appraise God with His true appraisal; the same measure root judges a false estimate of the One who measures creation.
Worldly enjoyment is called little and the Hereafter better for the God-fearing, another explicit comparison of the near share with the final one.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran whoever fears the warning, specifying fear as the condition that makes reminder reach its addressee.
The sun and moon move by exact calculation, a compact repeated formulation of celestial bodies governed by measure.
God subjects the sun and moon, each running to an appointed term, and directs the affair; created motion is aimed toward a fixed endpoint.
“Every thing We have enumerated in a record” gives a nonlexical parallel for creation in which nothing escapes prior count.
People have benefits and drinks from the cattle God subjected to them; this cautiously links the animal source, benefit, and drink that converge materially in the section’s hide water vessel.
